2.text: performance, they took him out of the sleeping-room. Now they restore him

3.text: to his place. Before entering the house, his whole body must be smeared

4.text: over with ochre. After that, he recovers completely.

5.text: Told by Qoˊtêrg̣ɪn (man) in the village of Mɪˊs˙qᴀn, 1900.
5.note: Karpaiˊñin's neighbour Qoˊtêrg̣ɪn is a proper name not in the lexicon (below the two-page floor); dot below g and small-cap ɪ both confirmed at 4x.
5.as_typed: Told by Qoˊtêrg̣ɪn (man) in the village of {Mi_'s.qa_n}, 1900.

6.text: (d) If a man is suffering, there is an old bear, a Big Bear of the Time

7.text: of the First Creation. I make myself into that bear. All his hair is com-

8.text: pletely white, though he is no polar bear. I lick over my own fingers, and

9.text: catch with them the suffering man. At every spot where he feels pain I clutch

10.text: him tightly. Then I blow with force over his whole body, quite naked.¹
10.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B9, not the exclamation mark the machine draft read.

11.text: Told by a Reindeer Chukchee of the Kolyma Country.

12.text: (e) If I want to cure some one from disease, I transform him into earth,

13.text: and transform myself into a huge bear. I am strong; I am clawing the

14.text: earth, and scattering it around. Then I put the disease into the hole, and

15.text: cover it with the earth again. Thus I make everything tight.

16.text: Told by Scratching-Woman (man) at Mariinsky Post, 1900.

17.text: (f) “The bird Karpaiˊñin! there comes Karpaiˊñin with iron quills, which
17.note: Italic sub-item letter (f) misread as a slash by the machine draft; corrected against the raster. Karpaiˊñin not in the lexicon (below floor); stress and tilde confirmed at 4x.

18.text: are very sharp.² He enters the mouth of the patient, and makes his
18.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B2.

19.text: dwelling-place inside of him. Inspect the liver, scratch it all over with your

20.text: iron paws, stab it all over with your sharp iron quills! Let the disease go

21.text: out from the neck, from the breast, from the stomach, from the whole body.”

22.text: After that, the patient paints his body all over with soot, which represents

23.text: the feathers of the iron bird.³
23.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B3.

24.text: Told by a Reindeer Chukchee of the Kolyma Country.

25.text: (g) For Pains in the Stomach. I call Kuˊurkɪl (the name of the Raven).
25.as_typed: (g) For Pains in the Stomach. I call {Ku'urki_l} (the name of the Raven).

26.text: This abdomen of mine I make into a bay of the sea. The bay is frozen,

27.text: altogether bound with ice. Plenty of rubbish is frozen there in the ice of

28.text: the bay; the rubbish is the disease of my stomach. “Oh! you, my stomach,

29.text: you are full of pain. I make you into a frozen bay, into a bad ice-floe,

30.text: into a very old ice-floe. Ho!” I call to Kuˊurkɪl. “You, Kuˊurkɪl, you
30.as_typed: into a very old ice-floe. Ho!” I call to {Ku'urki_l}. “You, {Ku'urki_l}, you

31.text: travel around from very remote times. I want your assistance. What are

32.text: you going to do with this bay? It is frozen. Mischievous people made it

33.text: freeze. You have a strong beak. What are you going to do?” Then the
33.note: Closing curly quote after 'do?' was dropped in the machine draft entirely; restored from the raster.

34.text: Raven breaks the ice through, but in reality it is the disease which is broken.

35.text: Everything that has stuck under the water I cause to be carried away; it is

36.text: floating on the surface. Then he comes⁴ to the man who asked for assist-
